claims.text: Molecular Dynamics simulations can be used to study the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The initial material consists of synthesized FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Particle size is varied in the Molecular Dynamics simulations.
The simulations are conducted at a constant pressure of 1 atm and a constant temperature of 300 K.
The simulations use a time step of 1 fs.
Atomic interactions are represented using an Embedded Atom Method potential.
Particle size and shape mediate the thermal response.
The thermal response involves thermal-energy transfer and atomic rearrangement.
Thermal-energy transfer and atomic rearrangement can be simulated by integrating the equations of motion using an EAM potential.
Thermal stability decreases as particle size decreases.
The nanoparticle melting point is reduced by at least 10% relative to bulk FeCuCrCoNi.
Particle size and melting-point reduction have a linear relationship with a slope of -0.5 K/nm.
The relevant nanoparticle-size range is 1–10 nm.
Particles in the 1–10 nm range are expected to exhibit thermal-stability behavior significantly different from bulk material.
The selected particle-size range is justified by theoretical models of nanoparticle thermal stability.
The accuracy of the EAM potential and the selected simulation conditions may affect the results.
The 1–10 nm size range may not capture the full range of thermal behavior.
The hypothesis is falsified if the melting-point reduction is less than 7% for particles between 1 and 10 nm.
The hypothesis is falsified if the slope relating particle size to melting-point reduction is greater than -0.2 K/nm.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify a constant temperature of 300 K, while the outcome and experiment require determining a melting point. No heating ramp or temperature variation is specified, so the stated fixed-temperature protocol is operationally incompatible with the melting-point measurement.
